listenerBrief: Ein verspielter Alltags-Podcast, kein Tech-Thema. Der Hörer Johannes isst Karotten und Kiwis ungewaschen mit Schale, kocht Hokkaido und Süßkartoffeln ungewaschen, kauft meist konventionell bei Lidl. Er will ein ehrliches Urteil pro Gewohnheit: Mythos oder wirklich leichtsinnig, und was er konkret ändern sollte. Leicht, witzig, neugierig, mit echten Zahlen, aber für Laien erklärt; jede Behörde und jeder Fachbegriff wird beim ersten Mal in einfachen Worten eingeführt. Kein Streitgespräch, Wissen teilen, mit einem klaren Fazit pro Lebensmittel am Ende.

editorBrief.rationale: Explainer: The material is a settled body of official data plus one listener question with a clear answer per habit — one host should walk it through, the other should ask the questions Johannes would actually ask. Nothing here is contested between two defensible positions; the only genuinely open points (no Lidl-specific data, green kiwi vs. SunGold peel numbers, no published exposure calculation for the sweet potatoes) stay open and are named as such, not staged. Deliberately different from the recent run: Jonas leads and explains after four episodes in a row where Lena carried the short formats, and the episode is built as four verdicts the listener can act on rather than as a decision briefing, a status report or a two-sided argument. At fifteen minutes it is longer than the last two short pieces because the magnitude reckoning and the germ section both need room, but far shorter than the twenty-to-fifty-minute project episodes.

roles.A: Jonas explains and leads. He carries roughly two thirds of the words: the two-limit distinction, the official numbers, the wash-and-peel efficacy, the germ section, and one verdict sentence per product. Calm, whole thoughts, numbers with anchors, never raises his voice.
roles.B: Lena is the listener's advocate and the reckoner. She asks the sharp questions — how much would he have to eat, what does washing actually remove, what about the green kiwi, what does this cost him in the kitchen at seven in the morning. She does not play the objection; every question is a real question and gets a real answer. She also owns the turn back to Johannes' own goals (fiber, folate, beta-carotene).

editorBrief.tone: De-escalating and concrete: it takes the fear out of the topic and puts the one real lever in its place. Sober where the numbers are, warm where the kitchen is.
editorBrief.opening: Straight in, no cold open, no number pile. Jonas's first sentence splits the question in two: there is a sales limit and there is a health limit, and almost every argument about pesticides mixes them up.
editorBrief.closing: The four verdicts again, short, one sentence each, as instruction rather than summary: what stays exactly as it is, what changes tomorrow morning, what he should stop. Then stop — no takeaway list, no outlook.
editorBrief.rhythm: Dense but conversational. Long stretches for Jonas in segment one and three, sixty to eighty words per turn, broken by Lena's number questions, not by acknowledgements. Segment two is the quickest: one product at a time, numbers, one pushback, one verdict, next product. Segment four slows down and lands.
devices: The running verdict line: after each of the four products, one short sentence that names the category — unbedenklich, ändern, einmalig prüfen. The listener asked for exactly this, so it earns the repetition.
One worked magnitude reckoning in segment one, using the listener's own body weight and one product, so 'how much would he have to eat' has a number instead of a shrug.
A named open point each time it appears ('das wissen wir nicht') — green kiwi peel data, no Lidl-specific evaluation, no published exposure calculation for the 219 sweet potato samples.
avoid: No staged disagreement or Gegenrede — the last four episodes leaned on an opposing-host or open-dispute format and the source here is not contested.
No decision-briefing framing ('alles entschieden außer …'), no Beschlussliste, no status report vocabulary.
Do not re-argue the Lidl question as a debate: name it once as structurally unanswerable, note that 78 percent of samples come from retail but are not broken down by chain, and move on.
No Öko-Test anecdote as a pattern — one test, five traces, all under the limits; if mentioned, only as an example of why single tests mislead.
No number-pile opening and no 'wait —' hook; no cold open built from statistics.
No scheduled jokes and no running gag across the episode; the material's humor is at most dry, in the everyday absurdity of eating a kiwi whole.
Do not read any list aloud — not the four products, not the washing percentages, not the to-do at the end.
editorBrief.glossaryPolicy: Introduce each body and term as what it is, then its name, one clause, only where it first matters. BVL as the federal office that counts what state labs find; BfR as the one that judges whether a finding matters; ARfD and Rückstandshöchstgehalt introduced early and in contrast to each other, because that contrast is the spine of segment one. Mepiquat and Chlormequat as growth regulators that keep plants short and standing, then the names, then the fact that they are not approved for fruit and vegetables in the EU. Toxoplasma, EHEC, spores and cucurbitacins each introduced at the point of use, never front-loaded. Where the notes transfer a number from one variety to another (SunGold peel data to the green kiwi), say so in the same breath.
